q: You `console.log(items)` inside `function f(items: any[])` and see `[{ id: 1, name: "Ada" }]`. What does that tell you about the *type* of `items` at the call site?
options: Nothing. Types are erased before the code runs, so the log only shows values
That TypeScript inferred `{ id: number; name: string }[]`
That `items` is a `Customer[]`, because the values match
That `any` was narrowed to the logged shape
explain: TypeScript types only exist while you write code; the JavaScript that runs has none. The log shows **values**. With `any[]` the compiler has already stopped tracking the type, and logging can't bring it back. To keep the caller's type, use a type parameter `T` in the signature.

q: Given `function ids<T extends { id: number }>(items: readonly T[]): number[]`, which calls compile? Select all that apply.
explain: The constraint is a **minimum**: each item must have *at least* `id: number`. Extra fields like `name` or `sku` are fine. `{ name: "no id" }` is missing `id`, and `{ id: "7" }` has an `id` of the wrong type (`string` isn't `number`), so both fail.

q: Both signatures accept a `Customer[]`. Why do the tests for *Dedupe by id* insist on the generic one?
code:
function a(items: { id: number }[]): { id: number }[]
function b<T extends { id: number }>(items: T[]): T[]
options: `a` returns `{ id: number }[]`, so the caller loses `name` and every other field. `b` returns `Customer[]`
`a` is slower at runtime because it checks every item
`a` doesn't accept objects with extra fields
explain: Types don't change runtime speed, so both run identically. The difference is what the **caller** gets back. `a` promises only the minimum shape, so `a(customers)[0].name` is a compile error. `b` passes the caller's exact type through: `T = Customer` in, `Customer[]` out. (And `a` does accept extra fields. Excess-property checks only apply to inline object literals assigned directly to a type.)

`K` is inferred as the literal `"admin"`, so `T[K]` is `User["admin"]`, which is `boolean`. If the return type were `T[keyof T]`, you'd get the union of *all* the value types, `string | number | boolean`. Having `K` as its own type parameter is what keeps it precise.
